---
title: "Growth despite decaying eigenvalues"
date: '2026-11-22'
image: nonnormal.png
categories:
- numerical-analysis
- linear-algebra
---

If all the eigenvalues of a matrix are negative, then every solution of the
linear ODE system $u' = Au$ eventually decays to zero.  Does that mean the
solution shrinks from the start?

## A diagonal system

Start with two equations that don't interact:

$$
u_1' = -u_1, \qquad u_2' = -10\, u_2 .
$$

Each component decays exponentially on its own: $u_1$ like $e^{-t}$ and $u_2$
like $e^{-10t}$.  Since both components shrink, so does the length $\|u\|$ of
the vector $u = (u_1, u_2)$.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof psi1 = Inputs.range([0, 180], {value: 60, step: 1, label: "initial direction"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof t1 = timeControl(invalidation)
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
figure(solve(0, psi1), t1)
```

In matrix form, this system is

$$
u' = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 0 \\ 0 & -10 \end{bmatrix} u .
$$

The eigenvalues are the diagonal entries, $-1$ and $-10$, and the
eigenvectors point along the two axes (the dashed lines in the plot above).

## A non-diagonal system with the same eigenvalues

Now put a nonzero number in the upper-right corner:

$$
u' = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 30 \\ 0 & -10 \end{bmatrix} u .
$$

The matrix is triangular, so its eigenvalues are still the diagonal entries,
$-1$ and $-10$.  But its eigenvectors are no longer perpendicular.  One still
points along the horizontal axis, while the other is nearly parallel to it.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof corner = Inputs.range([0, 60], {value: 30, step: 1, label: "upper-right entry"})
viewof psi2 = Inputs.range([0, 180], {value: 60, step: 1, label: "initial direction"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
tex.block`u' = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & ${corner} \\ 0 & -10 \end{bmatrix} u`
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof t2 = timeControl(invalidation)
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
figure(solve(corner, psi2), t2)
```

This time the solution more than doubles in length before it decays.  The
arrows show why.  They split the solution into its parts along the two
eigenvectors, and each part shrinks, just as in the diagonal system: the green
one quickly and the blue one slowly.  But because the eigenvectors are nearly
parallel, the two parts are long and point in nearly opposite directions, so
at the start they almost cancel.  Once the green part has decayed, what is
left is the long blue one.

A matrix with perpendicular eigenvectors is called *normal*.  Only non-normal
matrices can make the solution grow like this.

Things to try:

- Press Play and watch the green arrow shrink, leaving the long blue one.
- Make the upper-right entry larger.  The eigenvectors become more nearly
  parallel and the growth becomes larger.
- Make it smaller.  At zero you have the diagonal system again.  Below about
  6, the solution doesn't grow from any starting direction, even though the
  eigenvectors aren't perpendicular.
- Start along one of the eigenvectors.  The solution doesn't grow.  Starting
  close to one gives very little growth.

The same mechanism lies behind the transient growth of powers of non-normal
matrices, which matters in the stability analysis of numerical methods, and
behind transient amplification in fluid flows whose linearizations have only
decaying modes.  A good reference is the book *Spectra and Pseudospectra* by
Trefethen and Embree.

This page is based on a
[Jupyter notebook](https://github.com/ketch/ODE-counterexamples/blob/master/Vinograd-Dekker-Verwer.ipynb)
that goes on to a more surprising example, due to Vinograd: if the matrix
changes in time, the solution can grow without bound even though the
eigenvalues stay fixed and negative.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
tMax = 3  // final time shown
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
// Exact solution of u' = [[-1, b], [0, -10]] u with u(0) = (cos psi, sin psi):
// u(t) = z1 e^{-t} r1 + z2 e^{-10t} r2, where the eigenvectors are r1 = (1, 0)
// and r2 = the unit vector along (-b, 9).
function solve(b, psiDeg) {
  const l1 = -1, l2 = -10;
  const n2 = Math.hypot(b, 9);
  const r1 = [1, 0], r2 = [-b / n2, 9 / n2];
  const psi = psiDeg * Math.PI / 180, u0 = [Math.cos(psi), Math.sin(psi)];
  // Solve [r1 r2] z = u0.
  const z2 = u0[1] / r2[1], z1 = u0[0] - z2 * r2[0];
  const parts = t => {
    const c1 = z1 * Math.exp(l1 * t), c2 = z2 * Math.exp(l2 * t);
    const p1 = [c1 * r1[0], c1 * r1[1]];
    return {p1, u: [p1[0] + c2 * r2[0], p1[1] + c2 * r2[1]]};
  };
  const path = d3.range(0, tMax + 1e-9, 0.005).map(t => {
    const {u} = parts(t);
    return {t, x: u[0], y: u[1], norm: Math.hypot(u[0], u[1]), slow: Math.exp(l1 * t)};
  });
  const L = 1.1 * Math.max(1, Math.abs(z1), Math.abs(z2), d3.max(path, d => Math.max(Math.abs(d.x), Math.abs(d.y))));
  return {r1, r2, u0, parts, path, L};
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
// A Play button and a time slider; changing the other controls doesn't reset it.
function timeControl(invalidation) {
  const n = 300, dt = tMax / n;
  const form = html`<div style="display: flex; align-items: center; gap: .75rem; flex-wrap: wrap">
    <button type="button" class="btn btn-sm btn-outline-secondary" style="min-width: 4.5rem">Play</button>
    <input type="range" min="0" max="${n}" step="1" value="0" style="flex: 1; min-width: 10rem">
    <output style="min-width: 5rem"></output></div>`;
  const [button, range, output] = form.querySelectorAll("button, input, output");
  let timer = null;
  const show = i => { form.value = i * dt; output.value = `t = ${(i * dt).toFixed(2)}`; };
  const stop = () => { clearInterval(timer); timer = null; button.textContent = "Play"; };
  range.oninput = () => show(+range.value);  // the input event then bubbles to the form
  button.onclick = () => {
    if (timer) return stop();
    if (+range.value >= n) range.value = 0;
    button.textContent = "Pause";
    timer = setInterval(() => {
      range.value = +range.value + 1;
      show(+range.value);
      form.dispatchEvent(new Event("input", {bubbles: true}));
      if (+range.value >= n) stop();
    }, 30);
  };
  invalidation.then(() => clearInterval(timer));
  show(0);
  return form;
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
// Phase plane and length plot for the solution from solve(), at time tNow.
function figure(sys, tNow) {
  const {r1, r2, L, path, parts, u0} = sys;
  const {p1, u} = parts(tNow);
  const blue = "#1f77b4", green = "#2ca02c";
  // The plots are drawn at this size and scaled by CSS to share the column:
  // side by side when it is wide enough, stacked on narrow screens.
  const size = 310;
  const circle = d3.range(0, 2 * Math.PI + 0.01, 0.02).map(s => [Math.cos(s), Math.sin(s)]);
  const phase = Plot.plot({
    width: size, height: size, marginLeft: 40, marginBottom: 30,
    x: {domain: [-L, L], label: null}, y: {domain: [-L, L], label: null},
    marks: [
      Plot.ruleX([0], {strokeOpacity: 0.2}), Plot.ruleY([0], {strokeOpacity: 0.2}),
      // eigenvector directions
      Plot.line([[-L * r1[0], -L * r1[1]], [L * r1[0], L * r1[1]]], {stroke: blue, strokeOpacity: 0.5, strokeDasharray: "4,4"}),
      Plot.line([[-L * r2[0], -L * r2[1]], [L * r2[0], L * r2[1]]], {stroke: green, strokeOpacity: 0.5, strokeDasharray: "4,4"}),
      Plot.line(circle, {strokeOpacity: 0.3}),
      Plot.line(path, {x: "x", y: "y", strokeOpacity: 0.5}),
      Plot.arrow([{x1: 0, y1: 0, x2: p1[0], y2: p1[1]}], {x1: "x1", y1: "y1", x2: "x2", y2: "y2", stroke: blue, strokeWidth: 2.5}),
      Plot.arrow([{x1: p1[0], y1: p1[1], x2: u[0], y2: u[1]}], {x1: "x1", y1: "y1", x2: "x2", y2: "y2", stroke: green, strokeWidth: 2.5}),
      Plot.dot([u0], {x: d => d[0], y: d => d[1], r: 4, stroke: "currentColor"}),
      Plot.dot([u], {x: d => d[0], y: d => d[1], r: 5, fill: "currentColor"})
    ]
  });
  const ymax = 1.05 * Math.max(1, d3.max(path, d => d.norm));
  const norms = Plot.plot({
    width: size, height: size, marginLeft: 40, marginBottom: 30,
    x: {domain: [0, tMax], label: "t"},
    y: {domain: [0, ymax], label: null, grid: true},
    marks: [
      Plot.line(path, {x: "t", y: "slow", strokeDasharray: "6,4", strokeOpacity: 0.7}),
      Plot.line(path, {x: "t", y: "norm", strokeWidth: 2}),
      Plot.ruleX([tNow], {strokeOpacity: 0.3}),
      Plot.dot([{t: tNow, n: Math.hypot(u[0], u[1])}], {x: "t", y: "n", r: 5, fill: "currentColor"})
    ]
  });
  for (const p of [phase, norms]) Object.assign(p.style, {width: "100%", height: "auto"});
  // y-axis label as a box in the empty upper-right corner (the curves decay toward the bottom)
  const yLabel = html`<div style="position: absolute; top: 12px; right: 24px; font-size: 1rem;
    padding: .1rem .4rem; border: 1px solid currentColor; border-radius: 4px; opacity: .85">${tex`\|u(t)\|`}</div>`;
  return html`<div style="display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; gap: 16px; align-items: flex-start">
    <div style="flex: 1 1 0; min-width: 260px">${phase}<div style="font-size: .85rem">The solution (filled dot),
      starting on the unit circle (open dot).  The arrows are its parts along the two eigenvectors (dashed lines):
      <span style="color: ${blue}">blue</span> decays like ${tex`e^{-t}`} and
      <span style="color: ${green}">green</span> like ${tex`e^{-10t}`}.</div></div>
    <div style="flex: 1 1 0; min-width: 260px"><div style="position: relative">${norms}${yLabel}</div><div style="font-size: .85rem">Solid:
      the length of the solution.  Dashed: ${tex`e^{-t}`}.</div></div>
  </div>`;
}
```
